title: Platform Invoke (P/Invoke) awareness without becoming a C++ shop
hook: Platform Invoke (P/Invoke) calls native functions in operating system or third-party dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from C#. Modern LibraryImport source generation replaces much hand-written DllImport marshalling — you still need to respect calling conventions, string encoding, and resource lifetime.

blocks.text: DllImport and LibraryImport declare extern methods implemented in native code. The runtime marshals parameters — strings as UTF-8 or UTF-16, arrays as pointers — and translates calling conventions. SkiaSharp, SQLite, and GPU libraries wrap P/Invoke in managed APIs. You consume those wrappers; you rarely write raw declarations except for OS utilities or legacy SDKs.

blocks.text: Every P/Invoke boundary is a bug surface: wrong charset corrupts strings, wrong lifetime leaks native handles, wrong thread model crashes SkiaSharp. IDisposable on managed wrappers exists because native resources are outside the garbage collector. Interview answer: know the boundary exists, use official wrappers, and read lifetime docs — not every team needs custom C++.

blocks.title: Boundary discipline
blocks.body: Treat native handles like database connections — short lifetime, explicit release, no finalizer reliance.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Wrong CharSet garbling strings. Holding native pointer after managed array is unpinned. SkiaSharp objects without using — native memory leak until GC finalizer.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: LibraryImport source generation emits trim-safe stubs at compile time — publish with PublishTrimmed and verify no MissingMethodException on interop entry points. Compare to legacy DllImport which relies on runtime marshalling tables that trimming can break. For Native AOT deployments, LibraryImport is the default path. Pin Span<byte> only for the native call duration; long pins show up as GC heap fragmentation in dotnet-gcdump POH segments.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Writing new DllImport when LibraryImport is available for trim/AOT. Holding a native pointer after the managed array is unpinned. SkiaSharp without using — native leak until finalizer. Saying P/Invoke is 'free' — marshalling and charset mistakes garble production strings.

interviewTakeaways: P/Invoke is the managed-to-native boundary — marshalling, charset, and pin lifetime matter.
LibraryImport source generation replaces DllImport for trim-safe, Native AOT-friendly interop in .NET 7+.
In production, verify LibraryImport entry points survive PublishTrimmed — DllImport tables may break.
60s: P/Invoke = native boundary. LibraryImport = compile-time generated stub. Span for short pin. SkiaSharp needs Dispose. Prefer NuGet wrappers.
Follow-up: what breaks when you trim a DllImport declaration that LibraryImport would have generated?
commonPitfalls: Writing new DllImport instead of LibraryImport gets you rejected on AOT/trim interviews.
Ansi vs Unicode string mismatch garbling hostnames and paths in production.
Strong answer: 'LibraryImport for new code. Span pin only for call duration. Official wrappers over raw P/Invoke. Dispose native wrappers deterministically.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: sharp and bcrypt use native code like SkiaSharp. C# P/Invoke is declared in C#; Node loads .node binaries built from C++. LibraryImport is like a build-time generated N-API binding instead of runtime dlopen tables.
Node ffi-napi passes Buffer pointers with manual lifetime. C# LibraryImport + Span<byte> pins only for the call — same discipline as keeping a Uint8Array alive while native code reads it.
